steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper on multi-task learning for estimating heterogeneous face attributes (ordinal and nominal), where homoscedastic uncertainty is used to weigh the task losses. Cover motivation, limitations of prior approaches, our idea, and the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Face attributes and applications
- Single-attribute methods and their limits
- Joint estimation approaches and their limits
- Correlation and heterogeneity of attributes
- CNN hierarchy and our multi-task approach
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Face attributes
  - face images: important cue for social interaction, much salient information
  - past 20 years: big advances in extracting attributes to determine identity
  - applications: video security surveillance, personality recommendation, social media (cite)
- Single attribute
  - most previous studies (cite): single attribute or separate model per attribute
  - complexity, computation -> not suitable for realistic applications
- Joint estimation
  - newer approaches exploit attribute correlations for joint estimation; still limited
  - Sun et al. (cite): same features for all attributes, ignore heterogeneity
  - Han et al. (cite): gave up lightweighting to explore correlations between heterogeneous attributes
- Correlation and heterogeneity (Figure 1)
  - mustache + short hair -> more likely male, less likely lipstick
  - age ordered; gender and race nominal
  - correlation helps robustness; heterogeneity needs suitable prediction models
- CNN hierarchy (cite)
  - lower layers: local common features (textures, edges), less semantic, precise localization
  - upper layers: category-related, rich semantic features
  - -> multi-task learning with deep CNNs for correlation + heterogeneity
  - shared low-level parameters, separate classifier per task
  - ordinal regression -> linear combination of binary classification subproblems
  - no manual tuning of loss weights as in previous studies (cite); homoscedastic uncertainty as task-dependent weight; captures noise and scale per task
- Contributions
  - DMTL for ordinal + nominal attributes, feasible in edge systems
  - ordinal regression as binary classifications, mitigates estimation bias
  - optimal loss-weight search via homoskedastic uncertainty

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Face images give a lot of salient information and they are an important cue for social interaction. In the past 20 years there have been big advances in extracting attribute information from face images to determine the identity of the subject. This is applied in video security surveillance, personality recommendation, social media, and so on.

But most previous studies only estimate a single attribute, or learn a separate model for every face attribute. Because of the complexity and the computational effort, this is not suitable anymore for realistic applications.

To solve these limitations, new approaches were developed that explore the correlations between attributes to estimate multiple face attributes jointly. These approaches also have some serious limitations though. For example Sun et al. used the same features for estimating all the attributes of a face, and ignored the heterogeneity between the attributes. Han et al. gave up lightweighting in order to explore the correlations between heterogeneous attributes.

- Figure 1: correlations and heterogeneities
  - mustache + short hair -> more likely male, less likely lipstick
  - age ordered; gender, race nominal
  - correlation -> robustness; heterogeneity -> suitable prediction models
- CNN hierarchy
  - lower layers: textures, edges, less semantic, precise localization; upper layers: category-related, rich semantic
  - our multi-task approach with deep CNNs
  - shared low-level parameters, separate classifier per task; ordinal regression as binary subproblems
  - homoscedastic uncertainty as task weight instead of manual tuning
- Contributions: DMTL feasible on edge systems; ordinal as binary classifications; uncertainty-based loss weights

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Face images give a lot of salient information and they are an important cue for social interaction. In the past 20 years there have been big advances in extracting attribute information from face images to determine the identity of the subject. This is applied in video security surveillance, personality recommendation, social media, and so on.

But most previous studies only estimate a single attribute, or learn a separate model for every face attribute. Because of the complexity and the computational effort, this is not suitable anymore for realistic applications.

To solve these limitations, new approaches were developed that explore the correlations between attributes to estimate multiple face attributes jointly. These approaches also have some serious limitations though. For example Sun et al. used the same features for estimating all the attributes of a face, and ignored the heterogeneity between the attributes. Han et al. gave up lightweighting in order to explore the correlations between heterogeneous attributes.

We can see in Figure 1 that there are rich correlations and heterogeneities among the multiple attributes of the face. For example, people with a mustache and short hair are more likely to be male and less likely to wear lipstick. Some attributes like age have an ordered pattern, and gender and race are nominal. Attribute correlation can be used to make attribute estimation more robust, but attribute heterogeneity also has to be handled by designing suitable prediction models.

CNNs have a hierarchical nature and this gives a way to express the correlation of heterogeneous face attributes. The lower layers of a CNN tend to capture local common features in the image, like textures and edges. These features have less semantic information but they localize the target precisely. The upper layers of the CNN on the other hand gradually learn features related to categories, with rich semantics. So we propose a multi-task learning approach based on deep CNNs that takes both the correlation and the heterogeneity of face attributes into account.

In this work the low-level parameters are shared across all the tasks and every task has its own classifier. We focus on ordinal and nominal face attributes, and we transform the ordinal regression problem into a linear combination of several binary classification subproblems, which makes estimating ordinal attributes simpler.

Specifically, we do not manually adjust the multi-task loss weights like previous studies do. Instead we treat the homoscedastic uncertainty as a task-dependent weight. This quantifies the noise and scale of each task and helps to find the optimal weights.

To sum up, the main contributions of this paper are:

- • We propose a Deep Multi-Task Learning (DMTL) approach to estimate ordinal and nominal face attributes and we verify that it is feasible in edge systems;

- • For estimating ordinal attributes, we treat the regression problem as a linear combination of a series of binary classification problems, which mitigates estimation bias;

- • We use the homoskedastic uncertainty to do the optimal loss-weight search for multiple heterogeneous attribute estimation tasks.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
As an important cue for social interaction, face images provide a variety of salient information. Over the past 20 years, significant advances have been made in extracting attribute information from face images to determine subject identity. This is applied to video security surveillance, personality recommendation, social media [1,2], etc.

However, most previous studies [3,4] are limited to estimating a single attribute, or learn a separate model for each face attribute. Given the complexity and computational effort, this is no longer suitable for realistic applications.

To address these limitations, new approaches have been developed that explore attribute correlations for the joint estimation of multiple face attributes. Even these approaches have serious limitations. For example, Sun et al. [5] used the same features to estimate all attributes of a face, ignoring the heterogeneity between attributes. Han et al. [6] gave up lightweighting to explore correlations between heterogeneous attributes.

As shown in Figure 1, we observe rich correlations and heterogeneities among multiple face attributes. For instance, individuals with a mustache and short hair are more likely to be male and less likely to wear lipstick. Attributes like age follow an ordered pattern, while gender and race are nominal. While attribute correlation can be used to improve the robustness of attribute estimation, attribute heterogeneity should also be handled by designing appropriate prediction models.

The hierarchical nature of CNNs provides a medium for expressing the correlation of heterogeneous face attributes [7]. The lower layers of CNNs tend to capture local common features in the image, such as textures and edges. These features contain relatively little semantic information but offer precise target localization. In contrast, the upper layers of CNNs gradually learn category-related features with rich semantics. We therefore propose a multi-task learning approach based on deep CNNs that takes into account both the correlation and the heterogeneity of face attributes.

In this work, we share the low-level parameters across all tasks and design a separate classifier for each task. We focus on ordinal and nominal face attributes, transforming the ordinal regression problem into a linear combination of several binary classification subproblems, which simplifies ordinal attribute estimation.

Specifically, we avoid the conventional approach of manually adjusting multi-task loss weights used in previous studies [8]. Instead, we treat the homoscedastic uncertainty as a task-dependent weight. This quantifies the noise and scale inherent in each task and facilitates the search for optimal weights.

In summary, the key contributions of this paper are:

- • We propose a Deep Multi-Task Learning (DMTL) approach for estimating ordinal and nominal face attributes and verify that it is feasible in edge systems;

- • In estimating ordinal attributes, we treat the regression problem as a linear combination of a series of binary classification problems, thereby mitigating estimation bias;

- • Based on the homoskedastic uncertainty, we realize the optimal loss-weight search for multiple heterogeneous attribute estimation tasks.

References:
[1] H. Proença, “The uu-net: Reversible face de-identification for visual surveillance video footage,” IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology , vol. 32, no. 2, pp. 496–509, 2021.
[2] X. Yin, Y. Tai, Y. Huang, and X. Liu, “Fan: Feature adaptation network for surveillance face recognition and normalization,” in Proceedings of the Asian Conference on Computer Vision , 2020.
[3] W. Cao, V. Mirjalili, and S. Raschka, “Rank consistent ordinal regression for neural networks with application to age estimation,” Pattern Recognition Letters , vol. 140, pp. 325–331, 2020.
[4] Z. Zhao, P. Qian, Y. Hou, and Z. Zeng, “Adaptive mean-residue loss for robust facial age estimation,” in 2022 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo (ICME) , 2022, pp. 1–6.
[5] Y. Sun, M. Zhang, Z. Sun, and T. Tan, “Demographic analysis from biometric data: Achievements, challenges, and new frontiers,” IEEE transactions on pattern analysis and machine intelligence , vol. 40, no. 2, pp. 332–351, 2017.
[6] F. Wang, H. Han, S. Shan, and X. Chen, “Deep multi-task learning for joint prediction of heterogeneous face attributes,” in 2017 12th IEEE International Conference on Automatic Face & Gesture Recognition (FG 2017) , 2017, pp. 173–179.
[7] M. D. Zeiler and R. Fergus, “Visualizing and understanding convolutional networks,” in Computer Vision–ECCV 2014: 13th European Conference, Zurich, Switzerland, September 6-12, 2014, Proceedings, Part I 13 . Springer, 2014, pp. 818–833.
